#287. The pros and cons of using your phone as a mobile hotspot

Skip the questionable coffee shop Wi-Fi and bring your own internet.

Whenever you're out and about with your laptop and you don't have a Wi-Fi network to connect to, a mobile hotspot can save the day. Thankfully, your phone can be used to share its cellular data connection with other devices, from your laptop to your tablet to your friend's phone. On iPhones, this feature is called Personal Hotspot; on Android devices, it's usually found under Hotspot & Tethering, depending on brand.

As remote work and travel keep more and more people away from traditional office spaces and your comfy home desk, it makes sense that more people need to connect to portable internet options. Of course, hotspot devices are available to buy, but more often than not flipping a simple switch on your phone's settings makes a lot more sense. Still, as appealing as this option is, there are some trade-offs that you should consider about using your phone, from battery drain to the cost of your data plan. It's not the end of the world by any means, but it's something that comes with both pros and cons, much like anything else in the world.

There are quite a few benefits to using your phone as a mobile hotspot. First of all, it's so convenient to set up your laptop on the table of your go-to coffee shop, grab your phone and turn on the hotspot feature before quickly connecting to it. Your phone now handles your internet sharing, as well as all the other things you use it for, like calls, texts and the endless list of apps without worrying about a second gadget to charge, update or remember to pack.

Using your phone as a mobile hotspot is also extremely useful because you can do this anywhere you go, whether you're connecting your own laptop or you're making it easy for your kids to play Roblox on your trip. This can also be cost-efficient because you skip the expense of a dedicated hotspot device and a potential extra data plan.

There's also another fact that should most definitely be mentioned here, and that's tied to online security. Using a mobile hotspot is a safer option because you control who connects to it. That's preferable to joining potentially unsafe open Wi-Fi networks any day of the week (and twice on Sunday). It's important, however, that you set up a strong password so random people can't join, and to make sure your hotspot uses WPA2 or WPA3 encryption. For someone who only needs a backup connection a few times a month, these benefits often outweigh the drawbacks of a dedicated device sitting unused in that tech drawer filled with cables and random gadgets.

The convenience of using your phone as a mobile hotspot does come with some downsides that matter the more you rely on it. One of the most obvious ones is that running a hotspot is quite power-intensive, so your battery will drop noticeably faster while it's active. This can be solved by quickly refilling that battery with the help of a power bank or your laptop's charger.

Besides battery drain, it's also worth considering your data plan limitations. If your plan has a hotspot data cap, exceeding it can dramatically slow your internet speed or cost you a lot more money at the end of the month. Of course, it all depends on what you'll be using your hotspot for because video calls and streaming will burn through that data cap quickly.

You should also be aware that sharing a mobile hotspot with multiple people may mean slower speeds for everyone. Every connected device shares that same cellular connection, so performance drops as more devices join. Just be sure to remember the risks of leaving it password-free. An unsecured hotspot is very much an open door for anyone nearby, and you never really know who poses a risk. So tighten that security with a strong password.

In order to activate the mobile hotspot on your Android device, pull down the quick settings panel and tap on the Mobile Hotspot icon. On most phones, long-pressing on the icon will take you directly to the configuration menu where you can name the network, set up a strong password and choose the frequency band (2.4GHz or 5GHz, or 6GHz on some new phones). Depending on your phone, you may also find options for the MAC address type and an automatic shut-off timer for when no one is connected to the network. The procedure is similar on iPhones. Open Settings, then Personal Hotspot (or Cellular, then Personal Hotspot). You'll need to turn on Allow Others to Join and set a strong Wi-Fi password.

For occasional use, using your phone as a hotspot is a practical option that often costs nothing extra as long as your plan includes hotspot data. It usually saves you money, doesn't require any extra purchases and gets the job done without issue. But if you're tethering daily, streaming video or connecting multiple devices for hours at a time, the downsides pile up fast. For such situations, a dedicated hotspot device may be the best option and worth the investment. You should review your data plan and your usage patterns before deciding on the best way for you.

#286. SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch

STARBASE, Texas—The black-and-silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontally until the last moment, when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about 1 foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#285. The oldest gadget in your house could be your home network's biggest security hole

Your home network is only as secure as its weakest link.

It may not seem like you would need to replace a perfectly functional 10-year-old connected camera in your home. However, your network is only as secure as its weakest link, and that's often a device that is so outdated it no longer receives updates from its manufacturer.

Many of us don't realize how often gadgets need to be replaced, and it's not just cameras. Security cameras should be replaced every five to seven years, with router manufacturer Netgear recommending a hardware replacement every four or five years. You'll know it's well beyond time to replace your router when you start experiencing slower connections. At that point, you may already be facing security concerns.

When outdated gadgets like these are compromised, they could be sending your data to bad actors or working as part of a botnet. In 2025, the FBI issued a warning that end-of-life (EOL) routers–devices that are no longer receiving software updates or security patches–are being compromised by cybercriminals. It's ultimately up to the consumer to perform a regular device audit to determine if routers, cameras and other smart devices pose a security risk.

Any connected device in your home that no longer receives bug patches and security updates may be a risk. Per a 2024 Consumer Reports study, most appliance makers don't tell consumers in advance how long they will offer updates to software. It found that of 19 major brands that make smart appliances, only three told customers how long they would maintain support, and even the longest promised about five years of updates, falling short of consumer expectations of 10.

Routers are also often at risk. A 2025 FBI warning stated that routers dated 2010 or earlier likely no longer receive updates and should be replaced. In this particular case, such gadgets were being targeted by malware called TheMoon, which infects routers to install proxies, so criminals can operate anonymously. TheMoon hack doesn't even require a password, instead exploiting open ports and a vulnerable script. Even if you have a strong password, an old router can be a risk.

Routers and other smart devices that have been hacked can be recruited as part of a botnet, a network of devices used to overwhelm websites with traffic to take them offline. A recent report from Cisco found that nearly 40 percent of the vulnerabilities attackers targeted most affected end-of-life devices, and about a third of exploited vulnerabilities were at least a decade old. The report focused on businesses, but the lesson applies at home too: Attackers keep targeting old hardware because it never gets fixed. Even if most of your cameras and routers are up to date, just one outdated device can allow bad actors to enter the network and compromise anything else connected to it.

The good news is you don't have to replace everything in your home. Start by taking stock of everything on your network. First, log into your router's admin page and go through the list of connected devices. You may find gadgets you have forgotten about, like an old camera, smart plug or even your fridge. Then, search online for whether the manufacturer still releases updates for each device. If your router no longer gets firmware updates or is considered an EOL gadget, it may be time to get rid of it. If your smart appliance is too old to get automatic updates, you can simply turn off connected features. Chances are you don't need them anyway.

The latest standard for router security is WPA3. To upgrade your router from WPA2, go to the router's admin page, find the wireless security setting and choose WPA3. Some older gadgets will struggle to connect after switching, so choose WPA2/WPA3 if you run into that issue. If there is no WPA3 option, it is time to replace the router.

To make your home network more secure in general, turn off remote management and use a strong password. Never use the default password that came with your router. Turn on automatic updates to ensure firmware is updated as soon as it is offered. Otherwise, you can put any old gadgets and smart appliances on a separate network so that, if they are compromised, they can't get to more important gadgets like your laptop or phone. It's worth noting, though, that the data stored on outdated gadgets is still vulnerable, so it's always best to replace old hardware for maximum security.

#283. How to clear the application cache on your Mac

Clearing app caches don’t necessarily make your Mac run faster.

Your Mac applications often store temporary files, called caches, to improve user experience. This is a recommended best practice that most developers follow to prevent apps from creating or redownloading the same files each time you use them. App caches include temporary files like image previews, downloaded content and other data that help apps launch quickly and serve content without additional processing.

For example, Google Chrome builds its app cache as you visit different websites. It caches parts of webpages, like images, which helps speed up load times when you visit the same website next time. However, the problem with leaving application caches unchecked is that it could continue taking up storage space even when an application no longer requires the cached files.

Although your Mac may manage these temporary files, there's no guarantee when this process occurs. Moreover, problematic app caches can contribute to glitches, like displaying outdated or inaccurate content. Knowing how to clear app caches on your Mac can help resolve issues arising from an outdated cache or reclaim storage space wasted on bloating caches.

Some Mac applications allow clearing app caches from within the app itself. For example, Safari and Apple Music include the options to clear app caches in their settings menu. However, this is not the case for every Mac app out there; you'll need to manually find their caches to delete them.

Your Mac typically stores application caches in ~/library/caches. Since the library is treated as a hidden directory, your Mac may not readily reveal it in the Finder. To view the library folder: Finder > command + shift + H > command + J > check "show Library Folder." Once in the library folder, press command + J > check "Calculate all sizes" to display folder sizes alongside folder names.

In the caches folder, look for the application cache you want to clear. You can distinguish third-party apps from first-party Apple apps from the folder names and prefixes. First-party Apple apps use the "com.apple" prefix in their bundle identifier, while third-party apps don't. Open the application folder in question and delete everything inside to clear its app cache. If an app cache doesn't exist in the caches folder, you can look for it in ~/library/containers. The containers folder includes apps that run in a sandbox, so their cache is also isolated. Whether your app caches are in caches or containers, you'll need to apply the same principle for finding and deleting them.

It's worth understanding that clearing app caches doesn't necessarily improve application performance unless your Mac is already running short on storage space. However, deleting app caches can help reclaim storage space and sometimes even resolve app glitches. When you launch an app after clearing its cache, you might notice the app taking longer to launch, and using it might feel sluggish. This happens because the app has to rebuild its cache all over again. However, once this process is complete, your app should feel smooth and snappy to use.

It is not recommended to indiscriminately clear app caches or build a maintenance routine that involves one. Your Mac apps rely on caches to ensure a smooth user experience. You should only ever clear app caches if you notice the app not behaving as expected or if an app is taking up too much storage space. Otherwise, it's best to leave app caches alone and let your Mac manage it at its discretion.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the company said in a post on X. "We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible."

Launch failures are always a risk, but amazingly, United Launch Alliance had never experienced one previously. Since the company formed in 2006 as a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, its Atlas V rocket has been famously dependable. Now, the company's more powerful, more complex Vulcan will be under review by engineers and is facing a possible grounding.

"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," United Launch Alliance wrote. "ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action."

Following a refuelling issue that scrubbed a Friday launch, it was eventually rescheduled for Sunday, November 15th at around noon ET. However, controllers called a hold at T-minus 20 seconds due to an unknown technical issue. The problem was resolved before the end of the launch window and the rocket roared off the pad at 12:40 PM ET.

The solid boosters, which caused problems on two earlier flights, appeared to work normally. However, the first-stage methane engines fired longer than expected based on ULA's estimated timeline, as Spaceflight Now pointed out. After the first stage separated, the hydrogen-powered Centaur upper stage engines came on line for a planned 12.25-minute burn. The anomaly apparently occurred during that phase, ULA said on its website.

As well as being a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the failed launch will be a blow to Amazon's Leo internet satellite system, intended to rival SpaceXSI's Starlink network. Leo has 38 Vulcan flights booked to launch its satellites, following eight successful Atlas V missions. Many of those are now likely to be delayed.

Amazon's other launch provider, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, suffered its own setback in May when its New Glenn rocket exploded on the launchpad. The company has 24 flights booked on that rocket.

The Federal Communications Commission required Amazon Leo to have 1,600 satellites in orbit by July 31, 2026, but so far it only has around 390 in service. The company still planned to have 3,232 satellites in orbit by July 2029, but that goal may now be harder to obtain. "No operator could have predicted that all three core heavy-lift launch programs... would experience repeated, concurrent scheduling slips severe enough to exhaust the buffers Amazon Leo had built in," the company said back in July. With the failure of ULA's Vulcan on top of those delays, Leo can't seem to buy a break.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

#277. How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860

#276. Sony 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook review: A piece of PC history

It’s a perfectly adequate display with one unique hook.

It's an odd time for Sony to launch a PlayStation-branded gaming monitor, but hey, we'll take it. News broke in March that Sony would no longer bring its first-party games to PC, reversing course after a six-year run on desktops and teeing up a summer of heartbreak in the video game world. On the heels of this decision, Sony debuted the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook, advertising it as a desktop-geared peripheral that's compatible with PC, PS5 and a lineup of PlayStation accessories. It's sleek, it's sturdy, it has a crisp QHD display that supports VRR and HDR, and it features a buttery screen that handles glare well.

At $349, the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook is a reasonably hot gaming accessory. But more than anything, it feels like a vestigial remnant of Sony's abandoned plans to infiltrate the PC space.

The DualSense monitor has a 27-inch IPS display with QHD (2,560 x 1,440 pixels) resolution and a 240Hz refresh rate that supports VRR. Here we have the first sign that this thing was originally designed for PC play: The PS5 and PS5 Pro max out at 120Hz, and the monitor's 240Hz cap was included with PC play in mind.

It supports HDR on the spec sheet, but with a peak brightness of 350 nits and no advanced local dimming, you're mostly getting a broader range of colors rather than the eye-popping highlights the term might suggest. There's also a stereo speaker built into the display, and while its output is slightly tinny and lacking bass as you'd expect, it's perfectly acceptable. Put simply, this is a pretty standard gaming monitor in 2026.

As far as inputs go, there are two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 1.4, two USB-A slots, one USB-C connection and a 3.5mm audio output. They're tucked into a divot on the rear of the monitor and pointed downward, with a clever cable management hook that can be popped out from the stand's neck, keeping things as organized as possible.

The monitor is compatible with PC, Mac, PS5 and PS5 Pro, plus it can hold and charge a DualSense or DualSense Edge gamepad. It also functions with the PlayStation Link adapter, which enables Sony's Pulse and Pulse Elite wireless headsets, Pulse Explore earbuds and Pulse Elevate wireless speakers (at least theoretically). The Pulse headset will hit the market this month, while the Elevate speakers were just recently delayed indefinitely, extending the last echoes of a grander desktop scheme.

The DualSense charging dock swings down from behind the screen and hangs below the frame, and it's actually the star of the show. It's truly cute and also incredibly useful. Having a dedicated, out-of-the-way spot to store and charge an often-used gamepad is clutch.

The DualSense monitor is a noticeable upgrade from both the 27-inch Samsung 1440p/144Hz TN display and the 24-inch Alienware 1080p/240Hz IPS display that I currently use. This improvement applies not only to gaming scenarios, but also your standard PC use cases, like working, creating, watching YouTube, scrolling Reddit and streaming Real Housewives.

Sony's marketing positions the monitor as a display for your desktop PS5, but this is an uncommon console configuration and it's one that I don't personally have set up in my home. So, I tested out the monitor the way most players will use it, as a PC peripheral that happens to hold and charge my spare DualSense. This worked out exceedingly well for my gaming habits, considering I play Overwatch on PC and PS5, and I prefer to use a DualSense for both (keyboard and mouse players, don't come for me). However, outside of this one title, I tend to use the Wolverine V3 Pro for my Steam games, and there's no place to adorably dangle any non-DualSense gamepad from Sony's latest display. This is also true for literally every other monitor, of course.

I plugged in a set of Creative Pebble speakers and my PC, popped my favorite DualSense Edge on the dock, clipped a Logitech camera and Elgato light to the top of the monitor, and I was good to go. The display naturally rests parallel to the stand neck and it can be tilted upward about 30 degrees, but not downward. The tilt action is fluid and it sticks in place well. Shifting the screen vertically is less enjoyable but still easy: Hold a button at the back of the neck and the monitor clicks into place at varying levels. If you want to lower it more than 21mm from the top, you have to hide the charging dock first.

There's a large sliding glass door beside my desk, providing ample opportunity to test the monitor's glare-management abilities. The DualSense display has an eggshell-like coating that eats light like it's late for dinner, and it maintains a bright, crisp image even in a sun-drenched room. Things only improve in dimmer conditions, and the monitor's 240Hz refresh rate is a dream compared with my previous cap of 144Hz. With 1440p resolution, VRR and up to 240 fps in-game, I don't find myself longing for 4K visuals while playing Overwatch or any other game. Of course, I'm not coming from a 4K monitor, so I would say that.

The monitor also looks great on the desk, with a wide and thin metal base, sleek cylindrical stand neck and subtle branding. Maybe my previous display was just severely unstable, but I find the DualSense monitor to be surprisingly sturdy, especially considering its minimal design. Say you share a desk with someone who has a habit of idly bouncing their legs throughout the day, intermittently shaking the entire workspace and sometimes even knocking over your aesthetically placed Sanrio figurines. (A totally random, hypothetical example, of course). The Sony Gaming Monitor holds up well to this type of abuse, wobbling just slightly even under extreme leg-bouncing conditions. It's far more stable than my previous monitor, and it doesn't make plastic creaking noises when it does sway. All told, it's a sturdy piece of equipment.

Sony's 2026 PlayStation-branded gaming monitor is sleek, clever and cute, and at $349, it's a solid investment for anyone who even occasionally uses a PlayStation controller at the desk. My final read on the dock is that it's dope: It charges and stores the DualSense in a cool way, and provides a function that no other monitor will have. Even if you don't ever pull the charging dock down, this is a capable and clean display.

Sony clearly started building the 27-inch DualSense monitor before reversing its plans to take over the PC space, so in many ways, this peripheral exists as a physical reminder of a future that will never be. You could say it's already a piece of gaming history, something that feels more ephemeral by the day.

#274. How to use your phone to find an Apple TV remote

Lost in the cushions again? Here is how to find your remote without buying a new one.

Is there anyone in the world who owns a TV and hasn't lost the remote at least once? Unlikely, right? Now that remotes are slimmer and more compact, it's an even more prevalent occurrence. Losing your Apple TV remote is just as easy, of course. It can slip between couch cushions, end up under the blankets or get left somewhere when someone gets up from the couch to grab some water. The good news, however, is that your smartphone can actually help you find your Apple TV remote anywhere in your home.

Apple has a dedicated Remote app that will let you locate the device much like you'd use an AirTag. To find a missing Apple TV remote, you just have to pop open the app and hunt for the "Locate Remote" button, which will then trigger a beeping sound from the remote itself if you have the 2026 Apple TV 4K model. That helps if the thing's buried under the cushions.

In the meantime, you could also use that same Remote app to turn your phone into a fully functional Apple TV controller. Android users have some workarounds too. As long as your phone is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your Apple TV, you can regain control within minutes. You just have to know how.

If you've dug through the couch cushions, turned over every blanket, looked under the sofa and checked your kid's toy bins and still haven't found the remote, it's time to bring out the big guns. And by big guns, we mean to launch the Apple TV Remote app. This tool requires an iPhone running iOS 17 or later, while the Apple TV must have tvOS 17 or later. You have to open the Control Center on your iPhone and then tap on the Apple TV Remote. From there, tap the device list, tap Find and follow the prompts on your iPhone to locate your remote. The onscreen circle grows and grows and the text changes from far to near to here in a techy game of Hot and Cold.

The new Siri Remote that Apple released with its refreshed Apple TV 4K in October 2026 has Precision Finding hardware, which means it's easier to find with onscreen directional arrows and live distance guidance. There's even a built-in speaker that plays a chime to locate it. Previous models only come with proximity searching, so you'll have to rely on your phone to find the remote.

In case your remote is nowhere to be found and not even the built-in location feature is of help, then you have to try out a different method. You could, of course, order a new remote, but that's not absolutely necessary, and a new Apple TV is supposed to last long enough that losing a remote shouldn't push you to replace the whole setup.

To use the Apple TV remote, you just need to access your iPhone's or iPad's Control Center. As we already discussed, you have to tap on the Apple TV Remote button and then on your Apple TV or smart TV that's AirPlay-compatible from the list. You might need to enter a four-digit passcode to confirm the connection.

Once that's set up, you can use your phone as a TV remote to do things like control volume, open and close the device, switch streaming apps, control playback and so on. Everything you can do with the actual, physical Apple Remote, you can do with this app.

If you're an Android user, there's no official Apple-made remote app to use. There are, however, workarounds to replace your lost Apple TV remote without spending money. Third-party apps like Remote for Apple TV are available on the Google Play Store and replicate the core remote functionality of the physical remote. You'll need to download the app, ensure your Android phone is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the Apple TV and type in the onscreen code for pairing. Then you use the digital remote to hunt for your next binge-worthy show.

See? Losing the Apple TV remote doesn't have to derail your viewing session. The Remote app is the fastest and most reliable solution whenever you can't find the remote and you really want to turn down the volume or swap the app. Once you can hear your own thoughts again, you can resume your search for the device.

#272. Which Steam settings should you change to improve gaming performance?

Improving your system's gaming performance involves more than swapping components. Software can affect your frame rate as much as the system's hardware. Multiple overlays and background apps can quickly ruin your frame rate in any game. Even if you're selective about what you install, tried-and-true apps can slow your device down if you leave them on their default settings. A great example of this is Steam.

While it's a reliable gaming storefront with plenty of community tools, those tools can affect weaker machines or users on slow internet. By default, Steam starts when your system boots, loads community assets in the background and uses resources to power its in-game overlay. These small features can eat into your FPS and bandwidth, but the good news is you can turn almost all of them off to improve your gaming performance and system stability. The best place to start is Steam's overlay.

Steam's in-game overlay is a powerful tool. It gives you easy access to community guides, friend invites, frame rate limiters and in-game purchases. As useful as that can be, it comes at a cost: stability. Valve's overlay uses few system resources, lowering your FPS by maybe a couple of percentage points at most. However, many gamers can attest to just how buggy some titles are when the in-game overlay is enabled. With the overlay enabled, games might stutter, drop frames, or even crash. Disabling the overlay is generally a good place to start when these issues occur.

Open Steam and click the top-left corner, then select the "Settings" option. From here, go to the "In Game" tab to view all of your options with the in-game overlay. If you're experiencing major issues with most of your games, we suggest you toggle the "Enable the Steam overlay while in game" option at the very top of the menu. Your system will no longer use resources to run the overlay's background tools or web browser, saving bandwidth and improving overall system stability.

If disabling the overlay didn't fix the issue, Steam has a few performance settings you can toggle that should noticeably affect your FPS and bandwidth on weaker hardware. From the same settings menu, head to the "Library" section. There are two settings here that can help: Low Bandwidth Mode and Low Performance Mode. If you are having issues with graphical performance in general, we recommend enabling both and testing your in-game FPS. Should your frame rate improve, try disabling Low Bandwidth Mode and test again.

Low Bandwidth Mode disables Steam's background loading of community assets — community guides, artwork and video content. While this doesn't affect FPS directly, Steam can use a surprising amount of background bandwidth when this setting is disabled. For video games with online components or always-online requirements, leaving this setting on can improve your game's stability and frame rate.

The other setting, Low Performance Mode, disables some of the advanced graphic effects you'll find in Steam's library tab. It disables category transitions, game selection, and various icons to save system memory. This frees up system resources for whatever game you're playing, though it won't make a night-and-day difference on most systems. Pair this with disabling the in-game overlay to maximize your FPS.

#271. How Does a 74-Year-Old in Argentina Escape House Arrest on the Fifth Floor?

It involved a heating pad, animal fat and a bomb scare. The police are still looking for an Italian man facing extradition on 1970s-era terrorism charges.

By Zane Irwin and Lucía Cholakian Herrera

Zane Irwin reported from New York. Lucia Cholakian Herrerra reported from Buenos Aires.

Time was running out for Leonardo Bertulazzi. After decades of safe harbor in Argentina, Mr. Bertulazzi, once a member of a far-left terrorist group that kidnapped and murdered a former Italian prime minister in 1978, faced imminent extradition.

Back in Italy, a 27-year prison sentence for terrorism-related crimes awaited Mr. Bertulazzi, according to Argentina’s defense ministry.

Mr. Bertulazzi, 74, was placed under house arrest. The police were stationed across the street from the fifth-floor apartment he shared with his wife in Buenos Aires, Argentina’s capital. He’d had three strokes in the past two years, his lawyer said, and he was required to wear an ankle monitor.

None of that seemed to stop Mr. Bertulazzi from planning his escape.

On Tuesday, while much of the law enforcement apparatus of Buenos Aires was focused on the visit by Pope Leo, two police officers checked on Mr. Bertulazzi during a routine shift change, according to an official with knowledge of an investigation into Mr. Bertulazzi’s flight who was not authorized to speak publicly.

But this time, when the officers rang the apartment’s doorbell, nobody answered. Investigators believe Mr. Bertulazzi had escaped between 6 a.m. and 8 a.m. that morning.

Mr. Bertulazzi’s ankle monitor still showed he was at the apartment, the official said. A search revealed a metal box holding a mess of wires plugged into an outlet, prompting the officers to call an explosives disposal unit, according to the official.

#270. Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors

This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance’s 20-year history.

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents triggered monthslong reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”

“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”

Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”

The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.

Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’ Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’ chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

Vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#269. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#267. Hands-on (and off) with Mercedes-Benz's upcoming MB.Drive Assist Pro system

Benz takes us another step towards self-driving.

The streets of San Francisco are increasingly littered with oddly shaped cars festooned with bulbous sensors on the outside and no drivers on the inside. You can't go two minutes without seeing a car from Waymo or Zoox buzz by, proof that the autonomous revolution has hit the Bay Area. Still, those are all limited-use cars, summoned via smartphone, taking you to your destination, then disappearing from your life as quickly as they arrived.

When it comes to cars you can actually own, various manufacturers are making meaningful strides toward autonomy, but all in the form of driver assistance. These systems do some of the driving some of the time, but under the active supervision of the driver behind the wheel.

Next year, Mercedes-Benz is taking its own step forward with advanced driver assistance in the form of Hands-Free Highway Assist and MB.Drive Assist Pro. To get an early look, I visited that haven of autonomy for some laps of the Bay in the best that Mercedes has to offer.

My first go was behind the wheel of a GLS, Mercedes-Benz's largest and most luxurious SUV. In the high-performance AMG flavor, it's also reasonably fun to drive, but my job for the morning was to sit back and take my hands off the wheel.

Hands-Free Highway Assist is an upcoming feature that will let the driver go hands-free on limited, designated, divided highways. The driver will need to keep paying attention — an eye-tracking camera ensures that — but they can at least sit back and let the car handle the highway drone at speeds up to 85 mph.

I started in Alameda and made my way up to the 880, a highway still littered with the remains of the morning gridlock. Once there, I just turned on cruise control and waited for the visual indicators on the gauge cluster and heads-up display to change from a green steering wheel with green hands to a green steering wheel with gray hands.

That subtle cue proved to be the first problem. In the bright California morning sunlight, I struggled to spot the subtle color change on the HUD. On the gauge cluster, the indicator is positioned up in the corner, blocked by the steering wheel.

But eventually I spotted the signal, took my hands off, and that was that. The SUV and I just kept on going. It was entirely uneventful, which is exactly how these things are supposed to go. That didn't mean it was a completely passive experience, though. Traffic was thick and moving at various speeds across many lanes, and before long the GLS started to pick its way through, moving with intention and even aggression at times to maintain my chosen speed.

As my exit approached, it even changed lanes to the right, ensuring I was in as good a position as possible to get where I needed to go.

The automatic lane changes in the GLS generally worked well, but there was one moment when the SUV failed to detect a rapidly approaching car in the left lane and tried to change directly into its path. I had to grab the wheel to override.

Overriding is easy to do. There's none of the wrestling for control that some other assisted driving systems require. You just take the wheel and do what you like. The only issue I had was that after overriding the system, it often took 10 to 20 seconds before I could take my hands off the wheel again.

That's a far cry from other systems already on the road, like GM's Super Cruise. With that system, you just take the wheel, change lanes, then let go again. BMW's latest Highway Assistant in the new iX5 operates in much the same way, even applying the turn signal for you.

The other issue I had on the highway was frequent disengagements, where the GLS SUV would suddenly demand I put my hands back on the wheel even though there wasn't much going on.

Later in the day, I went out in an S-Class for a lap over the Bay Bridge, and things were even worse. I had at least a half-dozen disengagements during a roughly 45-minute loop. I was told that the system is being quite conservative to start, handing over control early whenever it sees a complicated situation is ahead. Hopefully that improves quickly, because the constant hand-offs made using the system more annoying than relaxing.

After my highway time, I got to meander through downtown San Francisco in a GLC SUV equipped with Mercedes-Benz's upcoming MB.Drive Assist Pro feature. This system works exclusively off the highway and requires hands on the wheel. You don't have to exactly be locked in at ten-and-two, but at least some constant contact with the steering is needed.

Do that, and the car basically drives itself, working its way through traffic, navigating intersections and roundabouts, avoiding jaywalkers, and basically doing everything needed to do to survive in a bustling place like SF. Plug a destination into the integrated nav system, and it'll even handle all the turns.

I got a preview of this system last year while driving the CLA, but this year I got behind the wheel. San Francisco isn't perhaps the most manic city on the planet, but it's up there, full of double parkers and a remarkable number of people making U-turns with no warning.

The GLC, seeing the world through 10 cameras plus five radar sensors, handled it all without issue. It calmly navigated pedestrians (whether they be in or out of the crosswalk), cyclists and all manner of bad drivers. During my journey, which took nearly an hour, I only needed to intervene once, tapping the accelerator at one point when the car got stuck sitting at an intersection.

In terms of driving behavior, the only weirdness was the SUV occasionally stopping at an intersection, creeping forward and then stopping again. Otherwise, it was faultless. Conservative at times, moving cautiously through complicated situations, but never so slowly that I felt like a road hazard.

I was told that Mercedes is considering making this configurable, a sort of aggression slider that would allow you to tailor the behavior of your car to your mood at the moment. Starting on the slow-and-steady side, though, seems like the right approach.

I was hugely impressed by how well the hands-on, point-to-point system worked. It took all the stress out of driving on city streets and worked with an ease and assurance often lacking in a certain other point-to-point driving system with a misleading name.

I was less impressed on the highway. The frequent disengagements and limited operating domain mean that Hands-free Highway Assistant is well behind competing offerings from BMW, Ford and General Motors, despite not being released yet. It is coming soon, though. Look for it in the spring of 2027 on compatible cars, which right now includes the 2027 S-Class, GLS and AMG GT 4-door Coupe. It'll also be available as an option on the 2027 CLA, GLB, C-Class, GLC and GLE as part of the MB.Drive Assist system.

The MB.Drive Assist Pro point-to-point navigation feature is slated for release next year for 2027 CLA Electric, GLE, GLS and S-Class models, with the company promising more to come in 2028. Some California customers will get a chance to enter an early access program later this year. Specific costs for these features have not been finalized.

That might feel a little slow and limited since this tech is already prevalent on many other brands today. However, given the safety-related aspects of these systems and what can go wrong, sometimes being a little late to the party sounds just about right.

#266. What is an NFC tag and how does one work?

Some people think they're just thin AirTags, but they're not.

If you've stayed at a hotel in the past five years, chances are you've noticed that room keys have changed. Some of them are now credit-card-sized pieces of wood that somehow communicate with the door, while other hotels also allow you to use your phone to unlock the door. Some allow both. This is all thanks to NFC, which is like the slick and cool child of RFID technology (the tech used in pet microchips, among other things).

NFC works at a much shorter range than RFID, which actually makes it more secure, and it can talk both ways, which is the reason your phone can now act as the key. The NFC tags themselves are now so thin and cheap to produce that you can purchase a pack of several dozen NFC stickers for just a few dollars.

But what exactly is an NFC tag, what is it good for, and should you be careful with it?

NFC stands for near-field communication, and much like Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, it is a wireless radio standard that allows different devices to exchange information with each other, just like RFID. Both technologies use radio waves to send out information, but depending on the type, RFID signals can be read from up to hundreds of feet away. NFC only works over very short distances under an inch, which makes it perfect for tapping a credit card on a reader.

An NFC tag is just a tiny chip with a little bit of memory and an antenna. It has no battery, so it draws power from whatever reads it through magnetic induction, the same technology that charges your phone wirelessly. When the tag gets close enough to a reader, the reader energizes the tag and pulls the data from it in a blink.

Because NFC tags are so cheap and simple, they are often used to store simple little commands that can be executed automatically. Many smart-home owners use them as physical switches — tapping your phone over a sticker next to the exit can run an entire "leaving the house" scenario where the lights turn off, the blinds close, and the alarm is turned on. Restaurants might stick little NFC stickers on the tables that automatically allow the customers to connect to the Wi-Fi and open the menu on their phones.

The low cost of NFC tags and the fact that they can be placed anywhere so easily make them useful in a wide variety of use cases. They can be found on posters, business cards, ski lift passes and elevators. You scan them with your NFC-enabled phone, and it sends a command to open a webpage or activate a feature on your phone.

In the case of tap-to-pay, transit gates and hotel room keys, the opposite happens. Your phone functions as the NFC tag, and once it gets close enough to the reader, it then activates and sends the information stored on it. Apple only opened the iPhone's NFC chip to third-party developers with iOS 18.1, so apps beyond Apple Wallet can now do this too.

An NFC tag cannot track you. Some people think it is just a thin version of an Apple AirTag, but the two are very different. An Apple AirTag has its own battery, and it sends out a Bluetooth signal that nearby Apple devices can pick up and report back to the owner. An NFC tag has no battery, cannot send a signal on its own and can only activate when it's almost touching the reader. So a sticker slipped into your luggage or onto your jacket can't tell anyone where you are.

Should NFC be on? Most people tend to leave it on since it uses very little power and only activates at very close range. It also won't hand over your card details to a stranger brushing past your pocket; both Apple and Android phones need you to unlock your phone in order to activate the NFC capabilities, with the exception of Express Mode for transit cards, which skips the check on purpose so you can get through a gate faster.

If you want to turn off NFC anyway, on Android you can switch NFC off in Settings, under Connections or Connected devices, depending on the brand. On an iPhone, it's a different story: NFC on iPhone XS and newer is always on and can't be turned off.
