#214. Asian love ballads test Eurovision’s winning song formula.

Carmelle of the Philippines defeated 10 competitors at the first edition of the high-camp event in Asia, held in Bangkok.

The Eurovision Song Contest crowned its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that tested whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base could appeal to audiences in a new market.

Carmelle of the Philippines was declared the winner of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, beating out artists and original songs from 10 other countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The show was live-streamed on YouTube and broadcast by television stations across the region.

Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.

Asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.

But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.

“It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” said Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any new thing, it needs to find its roots.”

Two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.

The Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.

“Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green said. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”

Ballads: Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers. Read more ›

Fans: Our reporter spoke to some of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision. Read more ›

Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›

No shows: For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences, starting with China and India. Read more ›

As Thailand’s Mang and Daou waited to learn whether they had won, the 26-year-old Mang was shown onscreen crying as if she couldn’t take the tension. That’s the sort of emotion needed to make Eurovision’s expansion into Asia a success. Acts have to want the title. But the show will also need the big Asian nations -- India, Japan and China -- to buy in, and much could now depend on the reaction in the Philippines to Carmelle’s win. The event was far less spectacular than a typical Eurovision in Europe. It also featured far too many ballads for my taste, but it was a fun afternoon’s viewing.

Shiesam Flores, 27, a clerk from the eastern region of Bicol in the Philippines, has been watching the show at a party with her friends — and hoping that Carmelle would prevail.

“It was nerve-wracking, nail biting suspense!” she said. “But we know she would win! What a talent!”

The Philippines’ Carmelle wins the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, pushing Thailand’s Mang and Daou into second.

The crowd roared in disappointment as Malaysia got only 70 points from the public vote.

Thailand takes a massive lead thanks to the public vote, but the genius of this voting process is we won’t know whether the Philippines can overcome them until the last seconds.

The public gave Beatmosphere, from Bangladesh, just 19 points. They looked surprisingly happy after getting such a low total, and it’s now confirmed they’ve come in a distant last.

Dara has brought the Eurovision Asia trophy to the stage. It’s a sparkly gold microphone.

The public vote can be brutal, as some acts rapidly learn that few viewers liked them.

The jury votes are all in, and it’s close. The Philippines is first with 93 points, Vietnam second with 83 points and Malaysia third with 82 points. We’re about to learn how many points each country’s act received from the public, starting with the current last place act, Bangladesh’s beatboxing-heavy crew Beatmosphere. It has 16 points.

One of the best parts of Eurovision is how the public’s choice is often completely diffferent from those of the juries, so don’t worry if your favorite act isn’t top of the ranking after the jury votes are all in. The Philippine’s jury, the first we’ve heard from, just gave its 12 points to Malaysia. That doesn’t mean it’ll win

Fans are decked out in flags and sequins for the first-ever Asia Eurovision here in Bangkok.

The problem Eurovision has with interval acts like Jeff Satur is that their stagecraft, singing ability and melodies are often a million times better than the artists in competition. Satur, who has 1.4 million monthly listeners on Spotify and over five million Instagram fans, has dozens of camp dancers onstage and a statue of a dragon. He would have cruised to victory if he’d been in competition, especially because of his ability to hold high notes close to the range only dogs can hear.

Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, said that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.

He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.

“I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.

“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.

Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.

Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.

Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, said that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.

“The only reason I know any music from European countries is because I heard them on Eurovision,” he said. “Eurovision Asia makes sense because the musical cultures are distinct.”

Mr. Hudson said he still listens to Loreen’s “Euphoria,” which won the competition for Sweden in 2012.

It was also the first Eurovision that Drew Andrea watched from his home in Sydney. A year later, he got a passport to fly to Sweden for the 2013 edition, and has attended every final since. Coming to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia was much more affordable, he said.

“Asia understands the brief — the kitschy costumes, the dance music,” he said.

His top picks among the Asian performers were the Philippines’ Carmelle and Vietnam’s Toc Tien. “I think they hit the nail on the head with the song, staging, costume and traditional elements,” he said.

Luca Cian, a professor of marketing at the University of Virginia who grew up in Italy, said that Eurovision built a global fan base by offering a shared cultural experience.

“Millions of people across Europe watch it at the same moment,” he said. “Families have watch parties with food and drinks. There are public discussions. Rituals create community.”

Carmen Chung, a British accountant, said she hijacked her family’s holiday in Bangkok to attend Eurovision Asia with her brother Garry Chung, a banker who lives in Hong Kong. “We were raised on Eurovision,” she said of their childhood in Yorkshire.

European acts, she said, tend to copy whatever style of music won the previous year. “This year, because there are no expectations, everyone has just done their own thing,” she said. She and her brother said they were rooting for Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, a beatboxing group that will perform an a cappella love song.

Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said that about half of the tickets for Saturday’s final were purchased by “super fans” from outside Asia. Organizers have kept the inaugural show modest, with 11 participating countries and a 5,000-seat venue.

Mr. Andrea said he didn’t mind the small scale.

“I’m O.K. with humble beginnings as long as it keeps growing every year,” he said.

The Thai pop star Jeff Satur, a guest performer, got the high-camp memo.

The presenters are talking to the artists in the green room and trying to get them to talk excitedly about Bulgaria, the country that will host the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest. The winner tonight might get to perform at that event. That seems to be making this show less about Asia itself than a spin-off of the main Eurovision event

Eurovision voting involves two parts. Juries representing music industry professionals from each country are allocated half the votes, and the viewing public decides the other half. To try to build tension, the show always announces the jury votes first by going live to representatives from each country who reveals their top acts. In the European edition of the contest, some of those spokespeople are celebrities, and often they try to give mini speeches or make jokes. This part of the show is always awful. You have been warned.

There are a lot of European expatriates in this crowd. That much is obvious when Bulgaria’s Dara, the winner of this year’s Eurovision, takes the stage with her winning song, “Bangaranga.” Some fans even danced along with her choreography!

Mohamad Iqbal Dzulqarnain, an Aina Abdul fan in Kuala Lumpur, said he felt her performance was better than the recording version.

“She left no crumbs,” he said. “She is going to win the contest.”

For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia on Saturday had several notable absences.

For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — were not there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, was absent.

That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest was South Korea.

China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.

Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, said in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.

It’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia did not participate. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, said that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”

Not participating saved those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.

Just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.

Here at the watch party in Kathmandu, Pratik’s relatives are happy with his performance.

“His voice was cracking during the selection round in Nepal,” said Sunita Rai, his sister-in-law. “Today’s performance was much more powerful.”

His relatives have been on social media all night, urging their friends who live overseas to vote for him. (You can’t vote for your own country’s performer.)

The presenters have just announced a technical issue! When Laos’s Thinla performed earlier, she had an earpiece problem and was unable to hear her own music. So that explains why she sang so out of tune. They’re now playing a recording of an earlier performance to everyone to try to ensure the event is fair

Rizal Kamal, a senior adviser to the Arts, Live Festival and Events Association, an entertainment nonprofit based in Malaysia, said he felt that Aina Abdul was the right singer to represent the country at Eurovision.

“Aina is seasoned in major competitions and she knows how to wow both the judges and the audience,” he said. “I am filled with pride.”

Aina Abdul’s inventive wardrobe and her powerful voice sets her apart from the Asian peers, said Adriana Syuhaidah, a fan in Kuala Lumpur.

“She is the Lady Gaga of Malaysia,” she said.

When they sat down to plan the final show of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest in Asia, the organizers faced a challenge: How could they introduce variety when most of the entries were slow-paced love songs?

Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers.

“Europeans tend to prefer songs with a crescendo, a hook and a grand ending, but also a strong social message,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of contemporary Europe at the University of Luxembourg who is an authority on Eurovision.

“The audience doesn’t want to see an innocuous pop song,” he said.

Electro-pop and dance songs have featured heavily on the list of Eurovision winners over the past decade. In May, Bulgaria’s Dara won with “Bangaranga,” a dance-pop song inspired by her diagnosis with attention deficit hyperactive disorder. Nemo, from Switzerland, won in 2024 with an EDM opera about their nonbinary identity, while in 2018, Israel’s Netta won with “Toy,” a pop anthem about female independence.

Some countries hold a nationwide contest to select an artist and a song to represent them in Eurovision, while others leave the choice to Eurovision’s local broadcasting partner. Audiences in the Philippines voted for Carmelle in a televised competition, for example, while Vietnam Television chose Toc Tien.

The two are considered front-runners in the Asian edition, with their high-energy folk-pop songs about female empowerment.

Malaysia’s Aina Abdul, another early favorite, will showcase her powerful vocals in “Bluest Sky,” a ballad with an orchestral arrangement that is about a troubled relationship. The track is reminiscent of “Wasted Love,” an opera-techno song that won Austria the European title in 2025.

Pratik Himal Rai of Nepal, who got married this summer, said love was easy to sing about because it can be understood across borders and languages.

“It is love that holds the world together,” he said in an interview.

He will sing “Ananta Maya” in Nepali. Other Eurovision Asia artists blend English lyrics with their national languages.

In Europe, every winning song after 2022 has been in English. That year’s champion, Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra, sang in their own language on “Stefania,” a hip-hop track that interspersed a Ukrainian lullaby with rap verses and traditional woodwind instruments.

Winning songs tend to blend a country’s national instruments and musical motifs with internationally trendy pop, Mr. Vuletic said.

A traditional Bhutanese flute can be heard in “Lhayi Semo,” Nyendra’s love ballad. Monetrey’s “I Let You Go” uses a Cambodian bamboo xylophone and a tro, a string instrument played with a bow. A kulintang, a percussion instrument made of eight brass gongs, keeps the fast beat in Carmelle’s “Sobra-Sobra.”

#213. Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”

That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”

Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”

“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”

This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”

So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.”

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

#212. Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice

Ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and said he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”

For the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

#210. Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

#209. SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft

While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.

In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.

Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.

In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”

Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night.

“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday. When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”

“Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”

#208. Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?

We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”

“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”

Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.

Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days.

Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me  — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.

But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down

Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.

And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.

Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.

But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.

So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.

Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.

Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.

And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.

But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.

Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.

I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.

I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that  — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.

Tim:  I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.

Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.

Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.

People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.

Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?

Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

#207. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#204. Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market

Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.

In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

#203. Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health

Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.

The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.

The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.

Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.

Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”

The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week.

#201. Helsing backer Plural raises $1.1B to fund Europe’s next moonshots

Operator-led VC firm Plural has raised €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in new capital, joining a growing cohort of larger European funds that also includes Mundi Ventures’ Kembara and EQT-managed Scaleup Europe Fund.

Despite its size, Plural’s fundraise isn’t (only) for a growth fund: two thirds will go to its third early-stage fund, and one third to a new “opportunities” fund making select follow-on investments, TechCrunch learned from Plural partners Khaled Helioui and Carina Namih.

The two buckets are fixed, but the check size is not. Plural is “still very committed to being an early stage fund,” Namih said. But Helioui added that some of the early-stage “moonshots” it plans to back may require “raising a couple hundred million” to get off the ground.

“Moonshot” is an appropriate term to describe some of Plural’s portfolio highlights, such as Proxima Fusion and The Exploration Company — and its new fund will be looking for equally promising opportunities in energy, AI infrastructure, defense, health, and more.

Many of these are capital-intensive, but this is no longer stopping European entrepreneurs, especially second-time founders, and companies like Daniel Ek’s Helsing are “not isolated cases,” said Helioui, who backed the startup’s seed round alongside two Plural partners.

“If you’ve built and scaled a company, chances are, you’re more likely to be driven and passionate about having an impact on Europe’s ability to defend itself, procure its own energy, or own its operations and manufacturing, rather than just another app,” he said.

With bigger pockets, Plural will be able to keep up longer with the larger and larger rounds its portfolio companies have gone on to raise. It also made an effort to raise more of this capital from Europe, Namih said.

While Europe’s institutional LPs were, for a long time, more likely to back banker types than founders hoping to displace those bankers, the current shift towards Europe’s sovereignty and resilience creates tailwinds for Plural, whose office in Tallinn played a key role in its decision to invest in defense tech — including in a missile company, Hypersonica.

“The reality is today still, you have a different level of conversation and a different sense of appreciation of the urgency and the criticality of these topics depending on how far from the border to Russia you are,” said Helioui.

Two of Plural’s six partners are Estonians, and Skype alumni: Wise cofounder Taavet Hinrikus and Teleport’s Sten Tamkivi. However, there is more to Plural than Tallinn; the fund also has offices in London, where Helioui, Namih and Ian Hogarth are based; and in Paris, where it hired former Uber executive Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty as a full-time partner in October 2025.

According to a press release, each partner will lead a small number of new investments a year. These companies will then get access to Plural’s growing portfolio support, which already ranges from hiring and communications to finance, Helioui said. That’s another indicator that VC firms in Europe are increasingly starting to look like their U.S. peers.

#199. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#198. Zoox robotaxis are now on the Uber app in Las Vegas

Zoox robotaxis are officially available through the Uber app in Las Vegas, marking the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company’s first partnership with a third-party ride-hailing platform.

The launch on Monday is a milestone for both companies. Uber gets to add another partner to its app as part of its broader strategy to become the primary purveyor of autonomous vehicle technology in North America, Europe, and the Middle East. Uber has partnered with more than 30 companies developing autonomous vehicle technology for sidewalk delivery robots, self-driving cars, robotaxis, and drones — though not all of those have turned into commercial deployments yet.

For Zoox, the partnership and launch gives it access to more potential customers who might otherwise not try its robotaxi, a needed boost as it trails market leaders Tesla and Waymo.

The partnership is expected to extend beyond Las Vegas. Zoox will begin initial robotaxi operations in Los Angeles this year (introducing the robotaxi and opening rides to Zoox employees, family, and friends), but commercial service will not begin until 2027. Rides will be available via the Uber app next year as well.

For now, all eyes are on Las Vegas, Zoox’s first commercial market and a city where Uber has ambitious robotaxi plans.

The two companies also announced a multi-year partnership with MGM Resorts International: they’re rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts properties in Las Vegas. Uber and Zoox said they’ll work with MGM Resorts to improve pickup and drop-off locations, along with signage to help riders navigate sprawling MGM properties and find the robotaxis.

Earlier this year, the Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved a permit that allowed Uber to deploy up to 1,000 robotaxis in Clark County — home to Las Vegas — through its partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox.

Zoox’s addition to the Uber app comes with some initial limitations. Customers won’t be able to select a Zoox robotaxi — at least initially. Instead, people who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save ride may be matched with one of Zoox’s custom-built robotaxis once they hail a ride. Customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi by opting for autonomous rides through “ride preferences” in the Uber app’s settings.

Uber plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.

“Las Vegas will become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app,” he said on the call. “We will begin with limited fleets and expand supply over the coming months, with plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in our app.”

The plan to offer a dedicated autonomous option marks a shift in Uber’s approach to robotaxis, including its partnership with Waymo.

That exclusive partnership, which matches Waymo robotaxis with Uber riders in Austin and Atlanta, will end in January 2028. Waymo plans to offer its rides directly through its own smartphone app as it does in other cities. TechCrunch previously confirmed with Uber that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree.

And unlike its partnership with other AV developers, Uber told TechCrunch that it will not provide maintenance and other services for Zoox in the Las Vegas market.

#195. Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”

Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

#193. Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings

Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.

Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy, says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.

Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.

“We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”

Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,0000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.

Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.

The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said.

To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.

Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said.

The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.
